mount-everest.short_description: Earth's highest peak, on the Nepal-China border in Solukhumbu, Koshi Province, and the focus of the Everest trekking and mountaineering region.
mount-everest.description:
Mount Everest, known in Nepal as Sagarmatha, is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level. It stands in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal's Solukhumbu District in Koshi Province and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Its height was most recently measured in 2020 through a joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities as 8,848.86 m. The summit point itself is a border location rather than a visitor access point.

The mountain gives its name to the wider Everest region, a high-altitude landscape of glaciers, icefalls and deep valleys framed by peaks such as Lhotse and Cho Oyu. It was first climbed in 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, and it remains the central objective of Himalayan mountaineering. The region is also the homeland of Sherpa communities, whose villages, monasteries and mountaineering culture are part of the experience of travelling here, and the mountain sits within the UNESCO-listed Sagarmatha National Park.

Most visitors do not climb the mountain. They come to trek in the Khumbu, typically flying to Lukla and walking north through the Dudh Koshi valley and Sherpa settlements such as Namche Bazaar, with a long approach by road and trail from Jiri as an alternative. Treks lead to viewpoints and to Everest Base Camp, and the region combines high mountain scenery with a living Sherpa cultural landscape. Conditions, trail status and permits should be checked before travel.
notes: The 8,848 m figure on the UNESCO page reflects the older survey; the 2020 joint Nepal-China survey gives 8,848.86 m, which this description uses.
Summit coordinate is a border point, not a visitor access point; access context is described rather than a mapped entry.

sagarmatha-national-park.short_description: A UNESCO World Heritage national park in Solukhumbu, Koshi Province, protecting Everest, glaciers, deep valleys and Sherpa settlements.
sagarmatha-national-park.description:
Sagarmatha National Park is a protected area in the Solu-Khumbu region of Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province, in eastern Nepal. It was gazetted in 1976 under Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979. The property covers 124,400 hectares and spans an elevation range of about 6,000 m, from around 2,000 m up to the 8,848 m summit of Mount Sagarmatha, or Everest.

The park is an exceptional high-mountain area of dramatic peaks, glaciers and deeply cut valleys, encompassing the upper catchment of the Dudh Koshi River. Seven further peaks rise above 7,000 m. It is home to rare species including the snow leopard and the red panda, and its forests, grazing lands and river valleys support a distinctive Himalayan ecology. Most of the park lies above 5,000 m as barren high ground, with grazing land and a small proportion of forest below that.

What gives the park its particular character is that people live within it. More than 20 villages and several thousand Sherpa residents share the landscape with the protected wildlife, and their Tibetan Buddhist culture, monasteries and farming practices are recognised as part of the site's value. The park is the core of the Everest trekking region. Visitors walk through Sherpa settlements, past monasteries such as Tengboche, and along glacier-fed valleys toward base camp and viewpoints, with a buffer zone extending protection beyond the inscribed boundary.

everest-base-camp.short_description: The staging camp at the foot of Everest's climbing route in Nepal, reached on a multi-day trek through the Khumbu region.
everest-base-camp.description:
Everest Base Camp is the staging area at the foot of the climbing route on Everest's Nepalese, or south, side. There are two base camps on opposite sides of the mountain: the South Base Camp in Nepal, at an altitude of about 5,364 m, and the North Base Camp in Tibet, at about 5,150 m. The Nepalese camp lies in the Khumbu region of Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province, inside Sagarmatha National Park, at the head of the Dudh Koshi valley near the Khumbu Icefall.

It is not a settlement but a seasonal camp. During the spring climbing season it becomes a temporary village of tents used by expedition teams, guides and support staff, while in the trekking seasons it is a destination for walkers. The route to it follows a long-established trail through the Dudh Koshi valley, past Sherpa villages such as Namche Bazaar and Tengboche and through the national park, with high peaks, glaciers and icefalls along the way.

Most visitors reach the area by flying to Lukla and trekking north over roughly two weeks, with a longer approach from Jiri by road and trail as an alternative. The camp itself offers little view of the summit, so many trekkers continue to the nearby viewpoint of Kala Patthar for a closer look at Everest. Altitude is the central consideration on this route, and the trek is usually taken slowly with rest days for acclimatisation. Trail conditions and permits should be checked before travel.
notes: No coordinate assigned: an authoritative base-camp visitor point was not verified. Elevation (about 5,364 m for South Base Camp) comes from the Wikipedia 'Everest base camps' article; no official Nepali source was found that states it.

gokyo-lakes.short_description: A group of high-altitude oligotrophic lakes in Sagarmatha National Park, Solukhumbu, designated a Ramsar wetland in 2007.
gokyo-lakes.description:
The Gokyo Lakes are a group of high-altitude oligotrophic lakes in Sagarmatha National Park, in the Solukhumbu District of Koshi Province, eastern Nepal. They sit at an elevation of roughly 4,700 to 5,000 m and take their name from Gokyo Ri, the peak above them. In September 2007 the lakes and their associated wetlands, covering about 7,770 hectares, were designated a Ramsar site, and UNESCO lists the Gokyo and associated lakes among the Ramsar protections associated with the Sagarmatha World Heritage property.

Oligotrophic means the water is low in nutrients, which is typical of cold, high mountain lakes and gives them their clear, blue-green appearance. The lake system lies in the upper Dudh Koshi catchment in a landscape of glaciers, moraine and high peaks, with the Ngozumpa Glacier, one of the region's largest, close by. The lakes are among the highest freshwater lake systems of their kind, and the designation recognises their hydrological and ecological value within the national park.

Travellers reach Gokyo on a side route of the Everest trekking region, rather than on the main trail to Everest Base Camp. The walk climbs through Sherpa settlements along the Dudh Koshi valley and up to the lakes, where a small settlement of lodges stands beside the water. From the lakes, most visitors climb Gokyo Ri for wide views of Everest, Cho Oyu and the surrounding peaks, and some continue over the Cho La pass to link with the base camp route. The area is remote and high, so acclimatisation and current trail and permit information matter.
notes: Ramsar designation details (September 2007, about 7,770 ha) are from the Wikipedia Gokyo Lakes article; the Ramsar Sites Information Service page could not be retrieved directly. UNESCO's Sagarmatha page confirms the high-altitude Gokyo Lake was declared a Ramsar site in 2007.
The record's coordinate is a mapped point for the lake group and does not identify a single lake or access point.

kanchenjunga-conservation-area.short_description: A protected Himalayan area in Taplejung, Koshi Province, established in 1997 around the world's third-highest mountain.
kanchenjunga-conservation-area.description:
Kanchenjunga Conservation Area is a protected area in the Himalayas of eastern Nepal, in Taplejung District, Koshi Province. It was established in 1997 and covers about 2,035 square kilometres. It takes in the Nepalese side of Kangchenjunga, the third-highest mountain in the world, whose summit lies at 8,586 m on the border between Nepal and the Indian state of Sikkim, with its West and Kangbachen peaks falling inside Nepal's Taplejung District.

The conservation area lies in the far east of the country and adjoins protected land on both sides of the border: the Qomolangma National Nature Preserve in Tibet to the north and the Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim to the east, and it borders Sankhuwasabha District. It forms part of the wider Sacred Himalayan Landscape, a conservation approach that links protected areas across the eastern Himalaya. The area spans a great range of altitude, from subtropical valley floors to permanent snow and ice, and holds forests, alpine pasture, glaciers and high peaks.

The landscape is also a living one, home to communities including Limbu, Rai and Sherpa people whose villages, monasteries and farmland sit within and around the protected area. Trekking here follows remote routes toward the Kanchenjunga base camps, passing settlement, forest, pasture and glacier on the way, and the area is quieter and less developed than the Everest and Annapurna regions. The temple of Pathibhara Devi, reached from the town of Phungling, lies nearby and is often combined with a visit. Boundaries, entry points and current permit arrangements should be confirmed with the responsible authority before travel.
notes: The Wikipedia article states the area 'comprises two peaks of Kanchenjunga'; that wording appears doubtful, so this description instead states that the West and Kangbachen peaks lie within Nepal, which is supported by the Kangchenjunga article.
Boundary, entry points and current trekking/permit information should be confirmed with DNPWC (record flagged needs_review).

ilam.short_description: A tea-growing hill district in Koshi Province, eastern Nepal, known for tea gardens, varied landscapes and cultural diversity.
ilam.description:
Ilam is a hill district in the far east of Nepal, in Koshi Province, with India's West Bengal to the east and Jhapa District to the south. The district covers about 1,703 square kilometres, and elevations within it range from roughly 140 m to 3,636 m above sea level, from lowland edges up to high ridge tops. Ilam town, also called Ilam Bazaar, is the district headquarters and is a quiet hill town in the Mahabharata range, acting as the base from which visitors explore the surrounding area.

The district is best known for tea. It is a major tea-producing part of Nepal, and much of the land is covered in tea bushes, with the tea industry growing and exports reaching markets in Europe and the United States. Alongside tea, the district's cash crops include cardamom, ginger, potato and broom grass, and the wider agricultural economy is diverse. Ilam is also described as one of Nepal's richest districts for cultural diversity and natural landscape, and it is called Charkhol, meaning area of four rivers, after the Jogmai, Puwamai, Mai and Deumai rivers that cross it.

A visit to Ilam is mostly about the landscape and the tea gardens. Walking through the tea estates, taking short hikes on gentle hills, picnicking in the gardens and visiting viewpoints are the typical activities, with Kanyam Tea Estate a well-known stop, and the Antu area associated with the Lepcha community, whose museum is being developed there. Mai Pokhari, a small lake with varied fish species, lies about an hour's drive from town, and Ilam Bazaar has hotels and a few tea-garden resorts that make it a base for day trips.
notes: Record represents the district/visitor destination, not a single geocoded attraction; the district elevation range (140-3,636 m) is not the elevation of Ilam town.
Deumai river name spelled 'Deaumai' on the Nepal Tourism Board page; spelled here as Deumai.

pathibhara-devi-temple.short_description: A hilltop Shakti Peeth pilgrimage temple in Taplejung District, Koshi Province, reached by a climb from Phungling town.
pathibhara-devi-temple.description:
Pathibhara Devi Temple, also called Mukkumlung, is a Hindu temple on a hilltop in Taplejung District, Koshi Province, in the far east of Nepal. The temple stands at an elevation of about 3,794 m and is reached from the town of Phungling, the district headquarters, by a climb of several hours. It is one of Nepal's Shakti Peeth, sites associated with the goddess, and is among the country's significant pilgrimage destinations.

The temple is revered by more than one community. For Hindus it is a shrine to Pathibhara Devi, a form of the goddess, and it is believed that a pilgrimage here helps fulfil a devotee's wishes, which draws worshippers from across Nepal and from India. Long before the present temple, a large rock on the hilltop was revered by the Limbu people, who follow the Mundhum tradition and see the hill of Mukkumlung as a natural form of their goddess, Yuma Sammang. In 1995 a Pathibhara Area Development Committee was formed, and in 2001 the sacred rock was replaced with a statue of the goddess. Pilgrims offer prayer, animal sacrifice, and gold and silver.

The temple sits on a forested ridge with wide views over the Taplejung hills and toward the Kanchenjunga range, and the walk up from Phungling is itself part of the visit. The temple is a side route to the Kanchenjunga trek, so it is sometimes combined with longer walking in the conservation area. Festivals and pilgrimage seasons bring the largest gatherings to the hilltop, while at other times the site is quiet and the climb can be cold. Access routes and current pilgrimage arrangements should be checked locally.
notes: Elevation of about 3,794 m is from the Wikipedia article and is not verified against an official Nepal source.

halesi-mahadev-temple.short_description: A cave temple in Khotang District, Koshi Province, held sacred by Hindus, Buddhists and Kirat communities.
halesi-mahadev-temple.description:
Halesi Mahadev Temple, also known as the Halesi-Maratika Caves, is a cave temple beside the village of Mahadevasthan in Khotang District, Koshi Province, in eastern Nepal. The temple and cave lie between the Dudh Koshi and Sun Koshi rivers, at an elevation of roughly 945 to 1,440 m, about 185 km south-west of Mount Everest. The main cave is a natural formation reached by steps below the surface, with a large chamber and further passages.

The site is unusual in being sacred to three traditions at once, which is why it is sometimes called the Pashupatinath of the east. Hindus know it as the Halesi Mahadev Temple and associate the cave with Mahadeva, a form of Shiva, who is said to have hidden there from the demon Bhasmasur. Buddhists consider it the Maratika cave associated with the legend of Padmasambhava, who is said to have attained the long-life realisation here, and the caves are referred to in Himalayan literature as early as the 12th century. The Kirati Rai of the region worship Halesi as an ancestral deity, and their Mundhum oral tradition links an ancestor to the cave, so it is also regarded as an ancestral place.

The cave is approached as a pilgrimage, with worshippers climbing through forested hills to reach it and then descending into the cavern. Well-attended fairs and festivals are held here, notably around Shivaratri, Bala Chaturdashi and Rama Navami, when pilgrims gather from across the region and from India. Outside festival times the setting is quiet and rural. The temple is served by road, and access by jeep or motorcycle is possible; local conditions should be checked before travelling.
notes: Elevation given on Wikipedia as 3,100-4,734 ft (about 945-1,440 m); converted here to metres.
Record lists alternate name 'Halesi-Maratika Cave'; the site is a group of caves and the associated temple.

koshi-tappu-wildlife-reserve.short_description: A Ramsar-listed wetland reserve in the Koshi river floodplain of eastern Nepal, important for birds and wild water buffalo.
koshi-tappu-wildlife-reserve.description:
Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve is a protected area in the Terai of eastern Nepal, covering about 176 square kilometres of wetlands in the floodplain of the Koshi River. It lies across the Sunsari, Saptari and Udayapur districts and ranges in elevation from about 75 to 81 m. It was established in 1976 and was designated a Ramsar site in December 1987, recognising the international importance of its wetlands. The reserve headquarters is at Kusaha.

The reserve is made up of extensive reed beds, freshwater marshes, grassland with patches of scrub and deciduous riverine forest, shaped by the shifting channels of the Koshi. It holds Nepal's last remaining population of the wild water buffalo, along with elephants, wild boar, hog deer, spotted deer, blue bull and jackal, and reptiles including the gharial crocodile; Gangetic dolphins are found in the Koshi River. Its birdlife is the reserve's other distinction: the Nepal Tourism Board lists 441 species, some of which migrate from as far as Siberia in winter, making the floodplain one of the country's foremost birdwatching areas.

A visit is centred on the wetlands and the river landscape. Activities are wildlife and birdwatching, typically on foot, by jeep or by boat along the river channels, with accommodation in resorts and tented camps near the reserve. The reserve is an easy add-on from Biratnagar, about a 90-minute drive away. The best seasons described by the Nepal Tourism Board run from October to March, alongside the hotter months of April to June and the rainy period from July to September, and current conditions should be checked before travel.
notes: Record had null province/district; the reserve spans Sunsari, Saptari and Udayapur districts. No single province is asserted here because the reserve crosses district boundaries.
Wikidata coordinate (26.65, 87) is not a visitor entrance; the description avoids implying a mapped entry point.

chitwan-national-park.short_description: Nepal's first national park, a UNESCO World Heritage site in the central Terai, known for rhinos, tigers, forests and Tharu culture.
chitwan-national-park.description:
Chitwan National Park is a protected area in the southern central Terai of Nepal and was the country's first national park, established in 1973. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984. The property covers 93,200 hectares and extends over four districts: Chitwan, Nawalparasi, Parsa and Makwanpur. It ranges in elevation from about 100 m in the river valleys to 815 m in the Siwalik hills. Because it crosses districts and present-day provincial boundaries, it is not attributed to a single province.

The park is the last surviving major example of the natural ecosystems of the Terai, the lowland belt that once ran along the Himalayan foothills of Nepal and India. It lies between the Narayani (Gandaki) and Rapti rivers to the north and the Reu River and the Nepal-India border to the south, over the Sumeswar and Churia hills, and adjoins Parsa Wildlife Reserve to the east. Its mix of alluvial floodplain, riverine forest and grassland is prime habitat for the greater one-horned rhinoceros, which the park holds in one of the world's largest populations, and for the Bengal tiger. It is exceptionally rich in species, with over 350 bird species recorded, and it is also the land of the indigenous Tharu community, with Hindu pilgrimage sites such as Bikram Baba at Kasara and Balmiki Ashram at Tribeni.

Visitors come for wildlife in a lowland river setting. Jungle safaris by jeep or on foot, canoe trips on the rivers, birdwatching and visits to Tharu villages and cultural performances are the usual activities, and a buffer zone with community-run tourism surrounds the park. Beeshazar and its associated lakes within that buffer zone were designated a Ramsar wetland in 2003. Current park rules, seasons and entry arrangements should be checked before travel.
notes: Area differs between sources: UNESCO gives 93,200 ha for the inscribed property, while the Wikipedia article gives 952.63 km2 (95,263 ha). This description uses the UNESCO figure.
Park crosses current provincial/district boundaries; province and district are left unassigned.
